units.text: INT. HUSBAND - CONTINUOUS
To SIR ROBERT CHILTERN.
You will go and write your letter to the Prime Minister now, won’t you? Don’t hesitate about it, Robert.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: With a touch of bitterness .
I suppose I had better write it at once. Such offers are not repeated. I will ask you to excuse me for a moment, Lord Caversham.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: I may come with you, Robert, may I not?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Yes, Gertrude.
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: LADY CHILTERN goes out with him .
What is the matter with this family? Something wrong here, eh?
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: Tapping his forehead .
Idiocy? Hereditary, I suppose. Both of them, too. Wife as well as husband. Very sad. Very sad indeed! And they are not an old family. Can’t understand it.
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: It is not idiocy, father, I assure you.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: What is it then, sir?
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: After some hesitation .
Well, it is what is called nowadays a high moral tone, father. That is all.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Hate these new-fangled names. Same thing as we used to call idiocy fifty years ago. Shan’t stay in this house any longer.
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: Taking his arm .
Oh! just go in here for a moment, father. Third palm tree to the left, the usual palm tree.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: What, sir?
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: I beg your pardon, father, I forgot. The conservatory, father, the conservatory—there is some one there I want you to talk to.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: What about, sir?
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: About me, father.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Grimly .
Not a subject on which much eloquence is possible.
units.name: LORD CAVERSHAM

units.text: No, father; but the lady is like me. She doesn’t care much for eloquence in others. She thinks it a little loud.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: LORD CAVERSHAM goes out into the conservatory .
LADY CHILTERN enters .
Lady Chiltern, why are you playing Mrs. Cheveley’s cards?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Startled .
I don’t understand you.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Mrs. Cheveley made an attempt to ruin your husband. Either to drive him from public life, or to make him adopt a dishonourable position. From the latter tragedy you saved him. The former you are now thrusting on him. Why should you do him the wrong Mrs. Cheveley tried to do and failed?
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Lord Goring?
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Pulling himself together for a great effort , and showing the philosopher that underlies the dandy .

Lady Chiltern, allow me. You wrote me a letter last night in which you said you trusted me and wanted my help. Now is the moment when you really want my help, now is the time when you have got to trust me, to trust in my counsel and judgment. You love Robert. Do you want to kill his love for you? What sort of existence will he have if you rob him of the fruits of his ambition, if you take him from the splendour of a great political career, if you close the doors of public life against him, if you condemn him to sterile failure, he who was made for triumph and success? Women are not meant to judge us, but to forgive us when we need forgiveness. Pardon, not punishment, is their mission. Why should you scourge him with rods for a sin done in his youth, before he knew you, before he knew himself? A man’s life is of more value than a woman’s. It has larger issues, wider scope, greater ambitions. A woman’s life revolves in curves of emotions. It is upon lines of intellect that a man’s life progresses. Don’t make any terrible mistake, Lady Chiltern. A woman who can keep a man’s love, and love him in return, has done all the world wants of women, or should want of them.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Troubled and hesitating .
But it is my husband himself who wishes to retire from public life. He feels it is his duty. It was he who first said so.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Rather than lose your love, Robert would do anything, wreck his whole career, as he is on the brink of doing now. He is making for you a terrible sacrifice. Take my advice, Lady Chiltern, and do not accept a sacrifice so great. If you do, you will live to repent it bitterly. We men and women are not made to accept such sacrifices from each other. We are not worthy of them. Besides, Robert has been punished enough.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: We have both been punished. I set him up too high.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: With deep feeling in his voice .

Do not for that reason set him down now too low. If he has fallen from his altar, do not thrust him into the mire. Failure to Robert would be the very mire of shame. Power is his passion. He would lose everything, even his power to feel love. Your husband’s life is at this moment in your hands, your husband’s love is in your hands. Don’t mar both for him.
units.name: LORD GORING

units.text: Enter SIR ROBERT CHILTERN.
Gertrude, here is the draft of my letter. Shall I read it to you?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: Let me see it.
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: SIR ROBERT hands her the letter .
She reads it , and then , with a gesture of passion , tears it up .
What are you doing?
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN

units.text: A man’s life is of more value than a woman’s. It has larger issues, wider scope, greater ambitions. Our lives revolve in curves of emotions. It is upon lines of intellect that a man’s life progresses. I have just learnt this, and much else with it, from Lord Goring. And I will not spoil your life for you, nor see you spoil it as a sacrifice to me, a useless sacrifice!
units.name: LADY CHILTERN

units.text: Gertrude! Gertrude!
units.name: SIR ROBERT CHILTERN
